title: Feelings
hook: pleasant, painful, neither; worldly and unworldly (MN 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, the charnel ground, and your line: this body too. Did you do the thing you'd been putting off? Day two hundred fifty-six, and the second foundation.

Buddhist teachers point to a moment that comes very fast: before a thing is even named, it already feels good, bad, or neither. A song starts, and before its name comes to mind, something may already have leaned in or pulled back. A smell drifts out of a kitchen: yes, or no. A text lights up your phone, and there's a little flicker of good or bad before you've read a word. That flicker is fast and easy to miss, and in the Buddha's teaching it steers what comes next. The Satipatthana Sutta makes it the second foundation. Today's word: vedana.
screen: `BEFORE YOU KNOW WHAT IT IS.` → `A FLICKER: YES OR NO.` → `THE SECOND FOUNDATION.`

segments.voice: Vedana is usually translated feeling, but it doesn't mean emotions like joy or anger. It means the feeling tone of any experience: pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. In Buddhist teaching, every sight, sound, smell, taste, touch and thought comes with one of the three. The sutta's instruction is simple. When feeling a pleasant feeling, the practitioner knows, I feel a pleasant feeling. When feeling a painful feeling, they know it. When feeling one that's neither, they know that too. Then a second layer. Each feeling can be worldly or unworldly. Worldly feelings are tied to ordinary things: the pleasure of good food, the pain of an insult. Unworldly ones come from practice itself: the quiet joy of a calm mind, or the ache of wanting to be free. And then, of course, the chorus: inside, outside, arising and passing away. Why does this get a whole foundation? Because in Buddhist teaching, feeling is the hinge. In the chain the Buddha called dependent origination, feeling gives rise to craving. Pleasant feeling tends to spark wanting more. Painful feeling tends to spark pushing away. Neutral feeling, the texts say, has ignorance lying behind it: it slips past unnoticed, and attention drifts off. If you can catch the feeling while it's still just a feeling, before it becomes a want or a push, you've found a gap. And in that gap, you get a choice.
screen: `NOT EMOTION: FEELING TONE.` · `PLEASANT, PAINFUL, NEITHER.` · `WORLDLY AND UNWORLDLY.` · `FEELING IS THE HINGE TO CRAVING.` · then, large: `PLEASANT, PAINFUL, NEITHER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your attention move around the body and the room. Each time something catches you, a sound, an ache, the warmth of your hands, a thought, give it one quiet label: pleasant, painful, or neither. Don't explain it. Don't change it. Just label and let it go. You may notice how many things are simply neither. That's normal. The bell holds the time.
Vedana. The feeling tone of every experience: pleasant, painful, or neither. The hinge between what happens and what we want.
Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Today, when you reach for your phone, catch the feeling tone just before you reach. Name it. Day two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Many insight meditation teachers have students note the feeling tone of experiences as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, since Buddhist teaching places vedana just before craving in the chain of dependent origination.

match.prompt: match each kind of feeling to an example.
pairs: the quiet joy of a calm mind
a plain moment, not good or bad

fork.setup: you taste something delicious and immediately reach for more. where in that moment does the sutta suggest looking?
options: at the pleasant feeling itself, before the reach.
fork.reveal: knowing the pleasant feeling as a feeling, before craving takes over, is the whole second foundation.

original.note: Pali vedanā: feeling tone, pleasant, painful or neither.

trapdoor: what you thought: vedana means your emotions.
what it means: the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of every experience.
what a scholar hears: in the twelve links of dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda), contact conditions vedanā, and vedanā conditions taṇhā, craving.

notes: Sāmisa/nirāmisa rendered 'worldly/unworldly'; the examples given for unworldly feelings follow common commentarial explanations (e.g. MN 137); please check.
The tendencies (pleasant → lust, painful → aversion, neutral → ignorance) follow MN 44; the script renders the third as 'boredom/drifting', a simplification. Confirm.
